strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reconstructing high-fidelity, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars from motion-blurred multi-view videos.

The proposed method integrates a physics-grounded sub-frame blur synthesis model with continuous B-spline pose trajectories, non-rigid pose adjustments, and inter-frame continuity regularization, effectively resolving temporal and directional ambiguities in motion blur.

High-quality benchmark contributions: the authors built a customized 12-camera synchronized hybrid-exposure capture rig to collect real paired blurry and sharp multi-view video sequences, alongside a standardized synthetic benchmark based on ZJU-MoCap.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and thorough ablation studies demonstrating clear quantitative gains (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and qualitative visual improvements over 2D deblurring baselines across various blur magnitudes and key hyperparameter choices.
weaknesses: Baseline evaluations rely almost exclusively on GauHuman as the 3DGS human avatar representation. Validating the framework on alternative dynamic Gaussian avatar representations (such as 3DGS-Avatar or Animatable Gaussians) would better demonstrate generalizability.

Averaging $T$ virtual sharp renderings per training step inevitably scales up rasterization cost and memory consumption, but the paper does not report training/inference runtimes or computational overhead compared to the standard pipeline.

Foreground-background blur bleeding: as acknowledged in Section 5.5 and Figure 8, the method relies on hard pre-computed masks (SAM), which struggle along blurry boundary regions where foreground and background pixels mix.

Presentation refinement needed: Section 2.1 contains duplicated text (the paragraph beginning 'In recent years, the deblurring paradigm has shifted...' is repeated almost verbatim in the fourth paragraph of the section).

strengths: Relevant and well-motivated problem: Addressing motion blur in articulated 3D human avatar reconstruction is a practical and challenging problem, as human movements frequently cause severe motion blur in multi-view capture setups.

Sound formulation of articulated blur formation: Extending continuous-time trajectory modeling (B-splines) and non-rigid joint offsets to the SMPL kinematic chain allows realistic sub-frame motion simulation and end-to-end optimization with 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Hardware setup and real-world benchmark: Constructing a synchronized 12-camera hybrid-exposure rig (with neutral density filters and varying exposure times) provides a valuable real-world testbed and dataset for this underexplored task.

Comprehensive ablation study: The experiments systematically evaluate the necessity of B-spline pose interpolation, non-rigid residual deformation, LBS weight refinement, shape optimization, and inter-frame temporal regularization across multiple blur levels.
weaknesses: Repetitive text and drafting oversights: In Section 2.1 (Related Work: Image & Video Deblurring), an entire paragraph ('In recent years, deblurring has shifted from traditional blur kernel estimation...') is duplicated almost verbatim on Page 2, indicating careless proofreading.

Missing evaluation on novel pose animation: Although the paper emphasizes reconstructing 'animatable 3D human avatars', all quantitative and qualitative evaluations focus exclusively on novel-view rendering of the training motions. Evaluating avatar driving fidelity on unseen motion sequences (e.g., from MoCap sequences) is necessary to validate animatability.

Absence of dynamic 3D deblurring baselines: The comparison is restricted to direct 3DGS training and two-stage 2D video deblurring pipelines. Recent dynamic 3D deblurring approaches (such as DyBlurF, cited in the paper) should be discussed or benchmarked to better contextualize 3D-aware deblurring performance.

Vulnerability to blurry segmentation masks: The pipeline relies heavily on pre-computed binary segmentation masks (EasyMoCap/Segment-Anything) derived directly from blurry observations. Motion blur inherently creates semi-transparent boundary blending with the background, leading to boundary truncation or silhouette artifacts that the model currently does not account for.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in dynamic human avatar reconstruction: recovering sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian avatars from motion-blurred video captures where subject motion induces severe degradation and ambiguity.

Technically sound formulation combining a physics-based 3D blur formation model with an articulated sub-frame motion model (B-spline interpolation plus non-rigid pose displacement) and an inter-frame boundary regularization loss ($L_{reg}$) that effectively resolves temporal direction ambiguities.

Strong experimental evaluation comprising both synthetic benchmarks (synthesized via RIFE interpolation on ZJU-MoCap) and a dedicated real-world multi-view dataset captured via a synchronized 12-camera hybrid-exposure rig (4 long-exposure blurry views, 8 short-exposure sharp novel views).

Thorough ablation studies analyzing the impact of pose interpolation, non-rigid deformation, shape and LBS optimization, number of virtual integration steps $T$, control knots $P$, and performance at non-middle sub-frame timesteps.
weaknesses: Noticeable textual duplication in Section 2.1: the two paragraphs detailing image and video deblurring ('In recent years, the deblurring paradigm has shifted...') on page 2 and page 3 are nearly verbatim duplicates, reflecting drafting and editing oversights.

Lack of analysis regarding computational complexity, training runtime, and GPU memory overhead. Simulating blur by rendering $T$ virtual frames per blurry capture during training naturally increases rasterization and backward pass cost; quantitative reporting of training time and memory vs. baseline GauHuman is missing.

The baseline comparisons are restricted solely to GauHuman (coupled with 2D video deblurring pipelines). Demonstrating or discussing applicability to other dynamic human representations (e.g., 3DGS-Avatar) would substantiate broader applicability.

Reliance on pre-computed segmentation masks (SAM) and lack of handling for foreground-background blur blending (as acknowledged in limitations), which can introduce border artifacts when fast-moving limbs blend with high-contrast backgrounds.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human avatars directly from motion-blurred captures where standard pose estimation and 3DGS reconstruction fail.

The proposed 3D blur formation model is technically sound and well-formulated, combining B-spline sub-frame trajectory interpolation, non-rigid residual deformation, and inter-frame geodesic pose continuity to effectively resolve directional and temporal motion ambiguities.

A dedicated real-world dataset was constructed using a 360-degree hybrid-exposure multi-camera cage (4 blurry cameras with ND filters, 8 sharp cameras), providing a valuable real-world testbed for the community.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, demonstrating clear quantitative and qualitative advantages over two-stage 2D-deblurring pipelines across synthetic and real benchmarks, supported by thorough ablation studies (control points, blur intensities, camera counts, and pose perturbation robustness).
weaknesses: Training efficiency and computational cost are not analyzed: rendering and backpropagating through $T$ intermediate virtual frames per training step increases GPU memory and runtime overhead, which should be explicitly reported and compared against baseline runtimes.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: the method is benchmarked against 2D video deblurring combined with GauHuman, but does not compare with recent dynamic deblurring neural field / Gaussian splatting methods (e.g., DyBlurF or BAD-Gaussians) adapted for articulated human sequences.

Dependence on parametric SMPL topology limits the ability to deblur and reconstruct high-frequency dynamic details outside the body surface, such as loose garments, hair dynamics, or handheld objects.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: Reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human avatars directly from multi-view blurry video frames, where existing 3D avatar approaches fail due to motion blur and inaccurate initial pose fits.

Well-motivated formulation: Modeling motion blur via physically grounded temporal integration of warped canonical 3D Gaussians, coupled with B-spline pose trajectory interpolation and learned residual pose offsets.

Principled solution to temporal ambiguity: The inter-frame motion regularization term (measuring geodesic pose distance across adjacent exposure windows) effectively addresses the bidirectional ambiguity inherent to motion blur.

High-quality evaluation and real-world rig: In addition to synthetic evaluations on ZJU-MoCap, the authors constructed a 12-camera 360-degree hybrid-exposure capture rig (with hardware-synchronized short and long exposures) providing genuine ground-truth evaluation, alongside a monocular smartphone demo.

Extensive ablation studies: Thorough analysis validating key design choices, including trajectory representation, knot count, number of integration steps, robustness to SMPL initialization noise, mask noise, and varying blur magnitudes.
weaknesses: Computational overhead is not reported: Synthesizing each blurry training frame requires warping and rasterizing Gaussians at T intermediate sub-frames (T=5), which substantially increases training time and VRAM footprint. A quantitative discussion of training time, peak memory, and rendering speed is missing.

Evaluation is restricted to a single avatar backbone: The method is integrated and compared primarily with GauHuman. Demonstrating applicability or baseline comparisons on another 3DGS human representation (e.g., 3DGS-Avatar or Animatable Gaussians) would demonstrate broader generality.

Handling of non-rigid dynamics and loose clothing: Because the sub-frame motion is primarily parameterized through SMPL skeletal kinematics and joint-driven displacements, fast non-rigid dynamics (e.g., loose garments, hair, accessories) cannot be accurately tracked across the sub-frame interval, leaving residual blurring in those regions.

Integration in non-linear color space: The formulation averages rendered frames directly in sRGB space rather than linear radiance, which can cause radiometric inaccuracies and unnatural energy accumulation in high-contrast/specular regions.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars from motion-blurred multi-view/monocular video inputs, moving beyond existing methods that assume high-quality, sharp inputs.

Formulates a physically sound 3D-aware blur formation model by discretizing exposure integration via virtual sharp intermediate Gaussian splatting renderings, paired with a B-spline sub-frame rigid sequential pose model and fine-grained pose deformation.

The inter-frame geodesic motion regularization loss effectively addresses the temporal directional ambiguity inherent to motion blur, preventing non-physical pose oscillations between adjacent exposure windows.

Provides a strong experimental benchmark featuring both a synthetic dataset and an impressive custom 12-camera synchronized hybrid-exposure multi-view rig (4 blurry with ND filters, 8 sharp for novel-view ground truth).

Comprehensive experimental validation and extensive ablations, thoroughly analyzing each module (interpolation, deformation, LBS offset, shape optimization, trajectory representations, number of knots, virtual frames, and mask robustness).
weaknesses: Computational overhead and training complexity: synthesizing $T$ virtual sharp frames per blurry capture scales rasterization and gradient backpropagation roughly linearly with $T$. The manuscript lacks runtime, training time, and memory consumption comparisons against standard baseline models.

Reliance on the SMPL kinematic skeleton: while the model refines SMPL parameters and LBS weights, complex non-rigid motion outside the SMPL kinematic tree (e.g., loose clothing, hair dynamics, handheld objects) cannot be effectively captured by the joint-based motion model.

Blur formation linearity: the exposure integration is computed as an average over non-linear sRGB values rather than linear radiance before tone-mapping/ISP, which can cause intensity deviations in high-contrast specular regions.
The network architecture details for the pose displacement module $G_{disp}$ and LBS refinement $\delta$ are only briefly mentioned as 'simple CNNs' without sufficient architectural specification.
